front: Dot the I's and cross the T's
back: To be meticulous; to pay careful attention to every detail
example: Before submitting the contract, make sure you dot the I's and cross the T's.

back: To accept the consequences of one's actions
example: He made a mistake at work and had to face the music.

back: In a difficult or overwhelming situation, often financially
example: After losing his job, he felt totally underwater with his debt.

back: To be naturally skilled at speaking or writing persuasively
example: She has a way with words — her speeches always move the audience.

back: To understand each other well; to share the same views or communication style
example: Once we aligned on goals, we were speaking the same language.

back: Children often resemble their parents in behavior or personality
example: He loves football just like his dad — like father, like son.

back: On the other hand; used to introduce a contrasting thought
example: I want to go out. Then again, I have a lot of work to do.

back: Directly from the original or most reliable source; firsthand information
example: I heard straight from the horse's mouth that she got the promotion.

back: A decisive test that proves the effectiveness or quality of something
example: The presentation was the acid test of his leadership skills.

back: Used to express the purpose of an object or action
example: This tool is for cutting wood.

back: Used to add emphasis by connecting two related positive ideas
example: She is not only smart but also incredibly hardworking.

back: Used to express surprise or admiration about the degree or extent of something
example: I am amazed at how quickly you learned this.

back: Expresses a wish or positive expectation about a future action
example: I hope to visit Japan someday.

back: By performing the action just mentioned; as a result of doing that
example: She worked extra hours, and in doing so, she completed the project ahead of schedule.

back: To end a conflict and make peace with someone
example: After years of disagreement, they finally buried the hatchet.

back: a favor de
example: She voted in favor of the new policy.

back: incansablemente
example: She worked tirelessly to finish the project.

back: precipitadamente; sin pensar
example: He rashly quit his job without having another one lined up.

back: de manera apresurada
example: The decision was made in a hasty manner and cost them dearly.

back: llevar a cabo; ejecutar
example: The team carried out the plan without any issues.

back: correctamente; como se debe
example: Make sure the equipment is properly installed before use.

back: al tanto; enterado de algo
example: Only a few people were in the know about the merger.

back: reducir; disminuir
example: She is cutting down on sugar for health reasons.

back: cuánto tiempo
example: How long have you been living here?

front: how it does it is not a concern
back: cómo lo hace, no es una preocupación
example: The system works — how it does it is not a concern right now.

front: but you have to sit absolutely still
back: pero tienes que sentarte absolutamente quieto
example: The doctor said: don't move at all — you have to sit absolutely still.

back: te lo digo; te lo juro (informal, para enfatizar)
example: I'm telling you, that movie is amazing.

back: mucho antes
example: This was decided far before the meeting even started.

front: even I would rather be watching
back: incluso yo preferiría estar viendo...
example: This lecture is so boring — even I would rather be watching paint dry.

back: ni de cerca; muy lejos de eso
example: He thought he was ready, but he was nowhere near that.

front: when do we get to see the sun
back: ¿cuándo podremos ver el sol?
example: It's been raining all week — when do we get to see the sun?

back: por defecto; automáticamente
example: Since no one else volunteered, she became the leader by default.

back: Expresses past habits or repeated actions (equivalent to 'solía' in Spanish)
example: When I was young, I would walk to school every day.

front: If needed, Alex would allocate additional resources
back: Example of 'would' for a past habitual or conditional action: Si fuera necesario, Alex asignaría recursos adicionales
example: In the past, if needed, Alex would allocate additional resources without hesitation.

back: Cowardly; lacking courage (informal)
example: Don't be yellow-bellied — just ask her out!

back: Works perfectly; produces the desired result
example: I added a drop of oil to the hinge and it works like a charm now.

back: si es necesario; en caso de ser necesario
example: Call me if needed — I'll be available all evening.

back: lanzarse de lleno a; dedicarse completamente a algo
example: After the breakup, she threw herself into her work.

back: obstáculo; impedimento
example: The lack of funding was a major roadblock for the project.

back: obstáculo; estorbo (más formal que 'roadblock')
example: His fear of failure was a hindrance to his growth.

back: aunque; sin embargo (al final de una frase para contrastar)
example: I like the idea. It's risky, though.

back: ojo agudo; capacidad de notar detalles
example: She has a sharp eye for design — she noticed the misalignment right away.

back: diez veces (mayor); multiplicado por diez
example: Profits increased tenfold after the product launch.

back: Used for emphasis or strong recommendation (equivalent to 'sí que' in Spanish)
example: Do make sure you call before arriving.

front: Do make sure you choose the correct time to say that
back: Example of 'Do + verb' for emphasis: asegúrate (enfático) de elegir el momento correcto para decir eso
example: Do make sure you choose the right moment — timing is everything.

back: turn down
example: I'll have to turn down the invitation — I have a prior commitment.

back: because of / due to
example: The flight was cancelled because of the weather.

back: pressing / urgent
example: I had to leave early because of a pressing issue.

back: brush up (on)
example: I need to brush up on my English before the interview.

back: keep track (of)
example: I use a spreadsheet to keep track of all my expenses.

back: Used after certain verbs (suggest, recommend, enjoy, avoid) instead of infinitive
example: I suggest meeting with them next week.

back: Following rules or instructions strictly; doing something exactly as prescribed
example: The new manager does everything by the book — no exceptions.

back: Used to introduce additional or unrelated information casually
example: By the way, did you know the meeting was moved to Friday?

back: An exclamation expressing frustration, surprise, or disappointment (informal)
example: Damn! I forgot my keys again.

back: Place something on a surface; stop holding it
example: Put it down gently — it's fragile.

back: Approaching a problem with creative, unconventional ideas
example: We need to think outside the box to find a solution to this challenge.

back: Used to connect two negative alternatives; neither one nor the other
example: Neither the manager nor the team was informed about the change.

back: To merit or be worthy of something (good or bad)
example: She deserves the promotion after all her hard work.

back: Although; even though — used to introduce a contrasting idea
example: While the plan is ambitious, it is also achievable.

back: Expresses a desire for something that is currently impossible or unlikely
example: I wish I could travel more, but I don't have the budget.

back: Expresses regret about a past action that did not happen (past perfect after 'wish')
example: I wish I had taken that job offer when I had the chance.

back: Expresses a strong wish or regret, more emphatic than 'I wish'
example: If only I had studied harder — I might have passed.

back: Expresses a preference for one thing over another
example: I would prefer to meet in person rather than on a call.

back: Used in formal contexts to announce bad news; 'regret to inform' = lamentamos informar
example: We regret to inform you that your application was not successful.

back: Used to express apology before delivering bad news
example: I am very sorry to tell you this, but the project has been cancelled.

back: tan pronto como podamos; lo antes posible
example: We will send you the report as soon as we can.

back: To recover from something; to move past a difficulty or loss
example: It took her months to get over the breakup.

back: To leave a vehicle or stop doing something; to escape punishment
example: Get off the bus at the third stop.

back: To want to do something; to be in the mood for something
example: I feel like grabbing a coffee — want to join?

back: To start working seriously and with determination
example: The deadline is tomorrow — we need to knuckle down and finish this.

back: Expresses the danger of something happening as a consequence; te arriesgas a
example: If you don't save your work, you risk losing everything.

back: To be accustomed to something; estar acostumbrado a
example: I am used to waking up early — it doesn't bother me.

back: Almost certain to happen; very likely to occur
example: With that much preparation, you are bound to succeed.

back: Used to give emphasis to a reminder or instruction; asegúrate de
example: Be sure to bring your ID to the interview.

back: Not expected to happen; improbable; poco probable que
example: He is unlikely to change his mind at this point.

back: Expresses a repeated or continuous action, often unintentional; sigo haciendo algo
example: I keep forgetting to bring my badge to the office.

front: People in the United States shake hands firmly, while people in France kiss on the cheek warmly
back: Example of 'while' for contrast between two cultural norms
example: People in the United States shake hands firmly, while people in France kiss on the cheek warmly.

front: What is the primary function of adverbials of manner?
back: To modify verbs by describing how an action is performed (e.g., quickly, carefully, with enthusiasm)
example: She spoke clearly and confidently during the presentation.

back: A noun or noun phrase placed next to another noun to identify or describe it, usually set off by commas
example: Mr. Jordan, the CEO of our company, will lead the meeting.

front: The five essential ingredients for effective communication
back: Clarity, brevity, context, impact, and value
example: A great message has clarity, brevity, context, impact, and value.

front: Mr. Jordan, the CEO of our company, will lead the meeting
back: Example of an appositive: 'the CEO of our company' identifies 'Mr. Jordan' and is set off by commas
example: Mr. Jordan, the CEO of our company, will lead the meeting.

back: To make small, restless movements out of nervousness or impatience
example: He kept fidgeting with his pen during the interview.

back: The feeling of nervousness before or during a performance or public appearance
example: Even experienced speakers sometimes struggle with stage fright.

front: What we needed WAS an effective leader who could motivate us all
back: Cleft sentence structure for emphasis: 'What + subject + needed + WAS + noun phrase' highlights the most important element
example: What we needed was a clear plan, not more meetings.

back: Hola
example: Hi! Good to see you.

back: Buenos días
example: Good morning! How are you today?

back: Buenas tardes
example: Good afternoon, everyone. Let's get started.

back: molestar; irritar
example: It really annoys me when people interrupt mid-sentence.

back: hasta ahora; hasta el momento
example: So far, everything is going according to plan.

back: profundizar en; explorar a fondo
example: Let's delve deeper into the data before making a decision.

back: ¿verdad?; ¿no es así? — question tag used after 'I am'
example: I'm next on the list, aren't I?

back: para que; de modo que — expresses purpose or result
example: I sent a reminder so that no one would forget the meeting.

back: de inmediato; ahora mismo
example: I'll take care of it right away.

back: confiar en; depender de
example: You can always rely on her to deliver quality work.

back: Hola
example: Hallo! Wie geht's?

back: ¿Cómo estás?
example: Wie geht's? — Gut, danke!

back: Buenos días / Buenas tardes (saludo formal general)
example: Guten Tag! Kann ich Ihnen helfen?

back: no solo ... sino también — adds a second, equally or more important point
example: Not only did she finish the task, but she also helped her colleagues.

back: Used to express a desire for something that is impossible or unlikely in the present
example: I wish I were rich.

back: Fairly well; better than average (informal)
example: How was the meeting? — Pretty good, actually.

back: It is better to do something late than not to do it at all
example: He finally apologized after three years — better late than never.

front: The more diverse the team members' backgrounds, the greater the collaboration and innovation we can expect
back: Example of 'the more ... the more' structure: expresses a proportional relationship between two things
example: The more diverse the team, the greater the innovation.

front: The more alignment between individual and company values, the higher the job satisfaction
back: Example of 'the more ... the higher' structure for expressing proportional relationships
example: The more alignment between values, the higher the job satisfaction and engagement.

front: The less a leader beats around the bush, the more likely things are to get done
back: Example of 'the less ... the more' structure; 'beats around the bush' = avoids the main point
example: The less a leader beats around the bush, the more productive the team.

back: To feel attracted or interested in something or someone
example: I am really drawn to her leadership style — she inspires confidence.

back: Describes a past state that no longer exists; solía ser / era
example: Laura used to be a really prominent leader before she retired.

front: If needed / If necessary / If required
back: Concise formal alternatives to 'if it is required/needed' — used in professional writing
example: If needed, additional resources will be allocated.

front: I had a colleague who would boast about his knowledge
back: Example of 'would' for past habits: describes something someone repeatedly did in the past
example: I had a colleague who would boast about his knowledge every single meeting.

front: When I first started working remotely, I would check my emails every 10 minutes
back: Example of 'would' for past habits when working remotely; 'would check' = solía revisar
example: When I first started working remotely, I would check my emails every 10 minutes.

front: In my previous job, I would stay late to finish reports before deadlines
back: Example of 'would' for past habits in a professional context; 'would stay' = solía quedarme
example: In my previous job, I would stay late to finish reports before deadlines.

front: My manager would always encourage us to take short breaks to stay focused
back: Example of 'would' for past habits of another person; 'would encourage' = solía animarnos
example: My manager would always encourage us to take short breaks to stay focused.

front: When I worked in a team, we would have brainstorming sessions every Friday morning
back: Example of 'would' for a past repeated event in a team context; 'would have' = solíamos tener
example: When I worked in a team, we would have brainstorming sessions every Friday morning.

front: In the past, when facing challenges, Alex would remain focused on the objectives
back: Example of 'would' for a past habitual response to a situation; 'would remain' = solía mantenerse
example: In the past, when facing challenges, Alex would remain focused on the objectives.

front: Rarely will innovative ideas be welcomed so enthusiastically
back: Inverted sentence structure after 'rarely' for emphasis; subject and auxiliary are inverted
example: Rarely will you find such dedication in a first-year employee.

front: Not only are their insights valuable, but they are also appreciated by the entire team
back: Inverted structure after 'not only' for emphasis; auxiliary 'are' comes before the subject
example: Not only is she experienced, but she is also a great communicator.

front: Not only does the manager articulate clear goals, but she will also keep the team motivated
back: Inverted structure with 'not only does' (present tense); 'does' is added and placed before the subject
example: Not only does he complete tasks on time, but he also mentors junior staff.

front: Rarely do you see such innovative solutions implemented with such enthusiasm
back: Inverted structure after 'rarely': 'Rarely + do/does/did + subject + infinitive'
example: Rarely do you see this level of commitment from a new team member.

front: Rarely do you see challenges addressed as proactively
back: Another example of inversion with 'rarely'; highlights an uncommon situation for emphasis
example: Rarely do you see challenges addressed so proactively in a startup environment.

front: Feeling overwhelmed by social pressures, many teenagers struggle with mental health issues
back: Participial clause expressing cause; 'feeling overwhelmed' modifies 'many teenagers'
example: Feeling overwhelmed by social pressures, many teenagers struggle with mental health issues.

back: Working hard to gain approval or belonging from others
example: Many teenagers spend their energy striving for acceptance rather than developing their own identity.

back: Trying to prevent being left out or rejected by a group
example: She changed her behavior, hoping to avoid social exclusion from her peers.

back: The effect that people of the same age or social group have on one's behavior and decisions
example: Peer influence can be positive when friends encourage good habits.

back: To avoid getting to the main point; to speak indirectly
example: Stop beating around the bush and just tell me what you want.

front: take the bull by the horns
back: To face a problem or challenge directly and with confidence
example: Instead of complaining, she took the bull by the horns and fixed the issue herself.

back: Despite that; nevertheless — used to contrast a previous statement
example: The campus was big, but even so, I could find my way around.

back: Used to say that something was true despite what was just mentioned
example: I was always organized, but even then, I struggled with time management in college.

back: Expresses that something was achieved but at a cost or with a specific condition
example: I was able to balance my social life and coursework, but only by sacrificing sleep.

back: Used to emphasize that something happened at a specific moment and not before
example: I had to write a paper, but it was only then that I realized I had just a week to finish it.

back: Used to introduce a contrasting or qualifying point after what was just stated
example: Having said that, social pressure also leads to stress and burnout.

back: 'Having said that' acknowledges a counterargument; 'but then again' presents a different perspective on the same topic
example: The plan is ambitious. Having said that, it could work. But then again, the budget is a real concern.

back: Informal phrase used to emphasize that you are telling the truth or giving reliable advice
example: Trust me — this shortcut will save you at least an hour.

back: A direct command asking someone to move closer to the speaker
example: Come here — I want to show you something.

front: If I had had more money, I would be richer
back: Mixed conditional: past condition (if + past perfect) + present result (would + base verb)
example: If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor now.

front: If I hadn't eaten so much cake, I wouldn't feel sick now
back: Mixed conditional: past action (if + past perfect) caused a present result (would + base verb)
example: If I hadn't stayed up so late, I wouldn't be so tired now.

front: I would be happier if I had said
back: Mixed conditional expressing a present result from a past action; 'would be' + 'if + past perfect'
example: I would be happier if I had said something earlier instead of staying quiet.

back: To deal with an issue immediately, right when it arises
example: It's always better to address misunderstandings on the spot so they don't escalate.

front: must have been (deduction about the past)
back: Used to express near certainty about something in the past; casi seguro que pasó
example: John must have been angry about the way Lisa corrected him in front of everyone.

back: Expresses regret about a past action that was wrong; no debería haber
example: I shouldn't have yelled at him. It was too aggressive.

back: Completely tough and emotionally resilient; showing no weakness or sentimentality
example: She's hard as nails — nothing seems to get to her.

back: Not related to the subject being discussed; fuera de tema
example: Let's not go off topic — we only have ten minutes left.

front: I was wondering if we could
back: A polite and indirect way to make a request or suggestion
example: I was wondering if we could meet later today to discuss the project.

back: A polite way to ask for information; '¿te importaría decirme...?'
example: Would you mind telling me when the registration for this quarter's training sessions starts?

back: Directly from the original source; firsthand and reliable information
example: I got the news straight from the horse's mouth — the CEO told me himself.

front: I propose that the team be promoted for their excellent results
back: Formal subjunctive structure: 'propose/suggest/recommend + that + subject + base verb (no -s, no -ed)'
example: The board recommends that the project be reviewed by an external auditor.

front: The professional development plan proposes that workshops be implemented
back: Example of formal subjunctive after 'proposes that'; 'be implemented' = sean implementados
example: The plan proposes that workshops be implemented to enhance employees' skills.

front: It is essential that the project timeline be followed
back: Formal subjunctive after 'it is essential that'; 'be followed' = sea seguido (no passive -ed form here)
example: It is essential that the project timeline be followed to ensure timely completion.

front: The proposal recommends that additional resources be allocated
back: Example of subjunctive after 'recommend that'; standard in formal writing and proposals
example: The proposal recommends that additional resources be allocated for research purposes.

front: The team leader proposed that a comprehensive report be completed by the end of the week
back: Formal subjunctive: 'proposed that + subject + base verb'; 'be completed' = sea completado
example: The team leader proposed that a comprehensive report be completed by Friday.

front: My brother, an accomplished pianist, will perform tonight
back: Example of an appositive: 'an accomplished pianist' renames and describes 'my brother'
example: My brother, an accomplished pianist, will perform tonight at the concert hall.

front: The tall basketball player, LeBron James, scored a lot of points
back: Example of an appositive: 'LeBron James' identifies 'the tall basketball player'
example: The tall and strong basketball player, LeBron James, scored a lot of points.

front: My favorite hobby, playing the guitar, keeps me entertained
back: Example of a gerund phrase as an appositive: 'playing the guitar' identifies 'my favorite hobby'
example: My favorite hobby, playing the guitar, keeps me entertained during weekends.

back: To resist or challenge an idea; to express disagreement or opposition
example: It's sometimes important to push back on ideas to explore other alternatives.

back: To disagree with something or find it objectionable
example: I'm afraid I take issue with your proposal — I don't think it will work.

back: To respond to an argument by presenting an opposing point
example: I tried to argue, but he countered that the plans were not finished yet.

back: To argue the opposite position to stimulate discussion, even if you don't believe it
example: I often play devil's advocate in team discussions to make sure we've considered all angles.

back: A noun or noun phrase placed next to another noun to identify or describe it, usually set off by commas
example: My colleague, a brilliant engineer, solved the problem in minutes.

back: Informal contraction of 'I bet I would have'; expresses certainty about a past hypothetical
example: Bet I would've failed that test if I hadn't studied.

back: A word, phrase, or clause that adds extra information to a sentence but is not essential to its core meaning
example: She sings beautifully. ('beautifully' is an adjunct — it adds information but the sentence works without it)

front: When did you move to Chicago?
back: ¿Cuándo te mudaste a Chicago?
example: When did you move to Chicago? — About three years ago.

back: To start discussing the most important facts or practical details
example: Let's stop with the small talk and get down to brass tacks.

back: Delicious; very pleasing to taste or smell (informal)
example: This pasta is absolutely yummy — what's in it?

back: Innovative or pioneering; leading to significant advancements or changes
example: The company's groundbreaking research changed the entire industry.

back: To display or exhibit something, highlighting its best qualities
example: The event was a great opportunity to showcase our new product.

back: A pesar de; used to introduce a contrast without affecting the outcome
example: Despite the initial price difference, we can move forward if we make some adjustments.

back: To make progress; to continue advancing
example: Despite the setback, we need to keep moving forward.

back: Un punto de inflexión; a moment when an important change begins
example: Winning that contract was a turning point for the company.

front: Cross that bridge when you come to it
back: Address a problem only when it actually arises; don't worry about it in advance
example: What if we run out of funding? — Let's cross that bridge when we come to it.

back: When we are sure something is NOT true or impossible, we use 'can't' — no puede ser que
example: He can't be the manager — he just started last week.

back: To get very excited and enthusiastic about a particular topic, especially technical ones
example: We totally geeked out talking about the new AI models.

back: A competitor or person expected to lose; someone at a disadvantage who defies expectations
example: Nobody expected them to win, but the underdog pulled off an incredible victory.
